summary: This note describes how the Endangered Species Act of 1973 handles private actions that may harm listed species. A private party submits a Habitat Conservation Plan (HCP) and, if approved by FWS or NMFS, receives an Incidental Take Permit (ITP) allowing a set number of incidental takes, which can be revoked and varies in duration. Because the permit is a federal action, other laws such as NEPA can apply, and public comment is solicited. If harm cannot be avoided, an agency can seek an exemption from the Endangered Species Committee, which requires five of seven votes.
one_line: Explains how Habitat Conservation Plans, Incidental Take Permits, and Endangered Species Committee exemptions work under the Endangered Species Act of 1973.
key_facts: A person or organization submits a Habitat Conservation Plan (HCP) to the agency, either FWS or NMFS.
If the HCP is approved, the person or organization is issued an Incidental Take Permit (ITP) allowing a certain number of takes of the listed species.
An Incidental Take Permit may be revoked at any time.
The San Bruno Habitat Conservation Plan/Incidental Take Permit is good for 30 years.
The Wal-Mart store permit in Florida expires after one year.
Because an Incidental Take Permit is issued by a federal agency to a private party, it is a federal action, so other federal laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) can apply.
A notice of the permit application is published in the Federal Register and a public comment period of 30 to 90 days begins.
The key question is whether a listed species will be harmed by the action and, if so, how the harm can be minimized.
If harm cannot be avoided, the project agency can seek an exemption from the Endangered Species Committee.
The Endangered Species Committee is an ad hoc panel of members from the executive branch and at least one appointee from the state where the project is to occur.
Five of the seven Endangered Species Committee members must vote for an exemption to allow taking of listed species.
